claims.text: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a simple solid-solution state has relatively low hardness and strength.
The relatively low hardness and strength are governed primarily by the absence of nanoscale precipitates or ordered phases that impede dislocation motion.
High chemical disorder in the homogeneous CoCrFeNiTi solid solution produces moderate solid-solution strengthening.
Uniform lattice distortion and chemical disorder broaden dislocation cores in CoCrFeNiTi.
Broadening of dislocation cores effectively lowers the Peierls barrier.
The reduced Peierls barrier facilitates dislocation glide, enhancing plasticity and machinability at the expense of yield strength and hardness.
The proposed baseline is a single-phase, equimolar CoCrFeNiTi solid solution with homogeneous elemental distribution and no significant precipitates.
A controlled heat treatment or slight compositional adjustment can induce nanoscale ordering or precipitation without substantially changing the overall equimolar composition.
Nanoscale ordered phases or precipitates act as obstacles to dislocation motion.
Induced nanoscale ordering pins dislocations and increases work hardening and strength.
Increasing strength through induced nanoscale ordering will reduce ductility.
Relative to the baseline, ordered or precipitation-containing CoCrFeNiTi will exhibit higher hardness and compressive or tensile strength.
Relative to the baseline, ordered or precipitation-containing CoCrFeNiTi will exhibit lower plasticity.
The baseline CoCrFeNiTi alloy has favorable ductility and machinability despite relatively low hardness and strength.
The hypothesis is limited to approximately 25 °C and moderate strain rates around 1×10^-3 s^-1 under elastic-plastic tensile or compressive loading.
At high temperatures or extreme strain rates, dynamic recovery or phase transformation may supersede the proposed mechanism.
Short-range chemical order may independently affect the mechanical response.
Failure of confirmed nanoscale ordering to produce a statistically significant strength and hardness increase with reduced ductility would falsify the proposed main-cause explanation.

contradictions.description: The comparison is described as using two equimolar CoCrFeNiTi sets, but one permitted intervention is a minor compositional adjustment. A compositionally adjusted sample is not strictly the same equimolar alloy and would confound heat-treatment or nanoscale-order effects with composition effects.
